subject: Assessing physical activity levels from accelerometer data

messages.author: 10ef9ab962b91e87
messages.subject: Assessing physical activity levels from accelerometer data
parts:
Hi
I read about the R package GGIR in http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/GGIR.pdf and would be really grateful with some assistance if at all possible on a particular area.

I should say at this point that I am clinical in background and my technical knowledge in this area is limited - hence reaching out for support!

I am trying to understand how to use raw x,y,z accelerometer data to assess physical activity levels in METs. My current understanding is that METs can be estimated from total counts per minute using any one of various equations, e.g. Swartz MET Rate = 2.606 + (0.0006863 * CPM) but I'm not sure about how to convert x,y,x data to counts (per epoch). 

I have identified the following formula: counts = (x2 + y2 + z2)0.5  (power 0.5) which I believe may be the answer (or at least part of the answer) but after extensive searching on the internet I have yet to find anything definitive.

I would be so grateful if anyone could provide me with any guidance/insight at all in this area or point me to any reliable references.

Many thanks in advance for any help you can provide!
Paul.

messages.author: 13568954e9b4ef4b
messages.subject: RE: [GGIR] Assessing physical activity levels from accelerometer data
parts:
Hi Paul,

This R-package provides tools to process the raw accelerometer data. The processed data can be used to estimate METs, but that is not the direct aim of the package. Note that estimating METs and estimating other measures of energy metabolism from accelerometer data needs to be done specific to sensor location and potentially also specific to study population. The term counts is mainly a term used for traditional non-MEMS accelerometers. I call these summary measures of acceleration ‘metrics of acceleration’ and not counts.

 

In function g.getmeta you can decide which metric you want to use. In function g.analyse you can estimate time spent in MVPA based on metric ENMO. Both functions are brought together in g.shell.GGIR.

 

See also a recent publication on MET estimation: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24887173

See also my publication on metric design: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23626718

See also a recent population study in which this R-package was used to estimate time spent in MVPA: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25361583

BW

Vincent
